introduction_markdown: Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board, General Certificate of Education Examination, Advanced Level, 0710 Biology 1, June 2019. Multiple choice question paper. Time allowed: one and a half hours. Candidates must not use mobile phones in the examination room. Answer ALL the 50 questions in this examination; all questions carry equal marks. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D. Decide which answer is appropriate. Mark only one answer for each question: if you mark more than one answer you will score a zero for that question. Avoid spending too much time on any one question; if a question is difficult, move on to the next one and come back to it later.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**Multiple choice questions** - choose the best answer, A, B, C or D.

**Directions for questions 21 to 28:** one or more of the responses (i) to (iv) is/are correct. Choose: **A** if (i), (ii) and (iii) are correct; **B** if (i) and (iii) are correct; **C** if (ii) and (iv) are correct; **D** if only (iv) is correct.

**Directions for questions 42 to 50:** there are two statements. Read through the statements and then choose: **A** if both statements are true and the second explains the first; **B** if both statements are true but the second does not explain the first; **C** if the first statement is true and the second is false; **D** if the first statement is false and the second is true.

questions.enonce_markdown: The transport of soluble end products of carbohydrate and protein digestion through the intestinal mucosa into the blood capillary of the villi is by:
questions.corrige_markdown: The soluble end products are glucose (and other monosaccharides) and amino acids. They cross the epithelium of the villus by two mechanisms. When their concentration in the lumen is higher than in the epithelial cells they move down the gradient by (facilitated) diffusion through carrier proteins. Once the gradient has fallen they are taken in against it by active transport, usually co-transport with sodium ions, driven by the Na$^+$/K$^+$ pump that uses ATP. They then leave the cell and enter the blood capillary. Osmosis concerns only the movement of water, and endocytosis, exocytosis and pinocytosis move bulk fluid or large particles, which is not how monosaccharides and amino acids are absorbed. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The following are associated organs of the digestive system in a mammal:
questions.corrige_markdown: The associated (accessory) organs of the alimentary canal are the glands that pour their secretions into it through ducts: the liver (bile, through the bile duct) and the pancreas (pancreatic juice, through the pancreatic duct), both into the duodenum. The spleen belongs to the lymphatic system and has no digestive role, which eliminates B and C. Salivary glands are also accessory glands, but teeth are structures of the buccal cavity (part of the canal itself), so the only pair in which both organs are unambiguously associated organs is the liver and pancreas. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Phase at which gastrin is stimulated to release HCL in the stomach is the:
questions.corrige_markdown: Gastrin is a hormone released by the G cells of the pyloric region of the stomach. In the gastric phase, the presence of food (protein breakdown products, peptides, amino acids) and the stretching of the stomach wall stimulate the G cells; gastrin enters the blood, returns to the stomach and stimulates the parietal (oxyntic) cells to secrete hydrochloric acid. The cephalic phase is a nervous reflex (sight, smell, taste, thought of food) acting through the vagus nerve before food reaches the stomach, the intestinal phase begins when chyme enters the duodenum and mainly slows gastric secretion, and a conditioned reflex is the learned trigger of the cephalic phase. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The optimum pH for the functioning of the enzyme pepsin is:
questions.corrige_markdown: Pepsin is secreted as inactive pepsinogen by the chief cells and activated by hydrochloric acid. It works in the stomach, where the pH is about 1.5 to 2, and its optimum pH is about 2.0. A pH of 7 suits salivary amylase and 8 suits the pancreatic enzymes in the duodenum, and pepsin is denatured at the alkaline pH of the small intestine. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Absence of this vitamin in the diet results in the deficiency disease known as scurvy.
questions.corrige_markdown: Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C (ascorbic acid). Vitamin C is needed for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine during the synthesis of collagen, so a deficiency weakens connective tissue and capillary walls and causes bleeding gums, slow healing of wounds and loose teeth. Lack of vitamin A causes night blindness, of vitamin B (B$_1$) beriberi and of vitamin D rickets. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two organelles with a double membrane are:
questions.corrige_markdown: Mitochondria and chloroplasts are each bounded by an envelope of two membranes (and have an inner membrane system, cristae and thylakoids). The Golgi body and the endoplasmic reticulum are made of single-membrane cisternae, and the centriole is a non-membranous structure of microtubules. The nucleus also has a double envelope, but it is paired with the centriole in option D, which has no membrane. Only option C has two double-membrane organelles. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: This organelle can self-replicate:
questions.corrige_markdown: Chloroplasts, like mitochondria, contain their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes and multiply by dividing in the cytoplasm, so they are described as self-replicating (semi-autonomous) organelles; this supports the endosymbiotic origin. Lysosomes and microbodies are produced by budding from the Golgi body and the endoplasmic reticulum and do not replicate on their own. Centrioles are duplicated once per cell cycle, but by assembling a new centriole beside an existing one and not through DNA replication, so the chloroplast is the best answer. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Bright colours in certain plant parts are made possible by the following organelle in the cells of that part:
questions.corrige_markdown: The red, blue and purple colours of petals and many fruits are due to anthocyanins, water-soluble pigments dissolved in the cell sap of the large central vacuole (sap vacuole). The colour of the sap depends on its pH. Chloroplasts hold chlorophyll and give a green colour, microbodies hold enzymes such as catalase, and plasmodesmata are cytoplasmic channels between cells. (Chromoplasts give yellow and orange colours, but they are not offered here.) **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the water potential and subsequent pressure potential of a plant cell with solute potential of its sap vacuole at -1300KPa, when equili librated with pure water?
questions.corrige_markdown: The water potential of the cell is the sum of its solute potential and pressure potential: $\psi_{cell}=\psi_s+\psi_p$. Pure water has a water potential of 0 kPa, so at equilibrium with pure water the cell also has $\psi_{cell}=0$ (no further net movement of water). Then $\psi_p=\psi_{cell}-\psi_s=0-(-1300)=+1300\ \mathrm{kPa}$. The cell is fully turgid: the positive pressure potential exactly balances the negative solute potential. The pressure potential cannot be negative here, and a water potential of $-1300$ kPa would mean the cell is not at equilibrium with pure water. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The function of the liver that results in the production of bile pigments is the:
questions.corrige_markdown: Worn-out red blood cells are broken down in the liver (and spleen). The haem part of haemoglobin is converted to biliverdin and then bilirubin, the bile pigments, which are excreted in the bile, and the iron is stored or reused. Deamination of excess amino acids produces urea, detoxification deals with substances such as alcohol and drugs, and neither gives bile pigments. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: break down of hormones and fats.

questions.enonce_markdown: The simplest and vacuolar pathways make use of:
questions.corrige_markdown: Water moves across the root cortex by three pathways: the apoplast pathway (through cell walls and intercellular spaces), the symplast pathway (from cytoplasm to cytoplasm) and the vacuolar pathway (through the vacuoles as well as the cytoplasm). The word "simplest" in the stem is almost certainly a misprint for "symplast". Both the symplast and the vacuolar pathways pass from cell to cell through plasmodesmata, the cytoplasmic strands that cross the cell walls. The cellulose cell wall is the route of the apoplast pathway only. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The following thickening patterns in the cell wall of a young dicot branch favours increase in length when growing:
questions.corrige_markdown: In the young, still elongating part of a stem the first xylem vessels (protoxylem) are laid down with lignin in rings (annular thickening) or in a helix (spiral thickening). The unthickened wall between the rings or turns can stretch, so the vessel is able to lengthen as the stem grows. Reticulate, scalariform and pitted thickening cover much more of the wall and are found in the metaxylem of regions that have finished elongating; they would prevent stretching. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The enzyme and vitamin necessary for blood clotting are:
questions.corrige_markdown: When a vessel is damaged, platelets and injured tissue release thrombokinase (thromboplastin), which in the presence of calcium ions converts the inactive prothrombin into the enzyme thrombin; thrombin then changes soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads that trap blood cells and form the clot. Vitamin K is needed by the liver to make prothrombin and other clotting factors. In the other options fibrinogen and albumin are plasma proteins and not enzymes, prothrombin is an inactive precursor, and vitamins A, B$_1$ and C have no part in clotting. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The maximum volume of air an individual can force out of the lung after a normal expiration is called:
questions.corrige_markdown: After an ordinary (tidal) expiration the lungs still contain air that can be driven out by a forced expiration. This extra volume (about 1000 to 1200 cm$^3$) is the expiratory reserve volume. Tidal volume is the air moved in a normal breath, the residual volume is the air that always stays in the lungs and cannot be expelled, and the inspiratory reserve volume is the extra air that can be taken in after a normal inspiration. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The respiratory surface of an insect is called:
questions.corrige_markdown: Air enters the insect through the spiracles into the tracheae, which branch into very fine tracheoles. The tracheoles have thin, moist walls, end in contact with (or even inside) the respiring cells and contain fluid at their tips, so oxygen dissolves and diffuses across their walls directly into the cells: they are the actual gas exchange (respiratory) surface. The spiracles are only openings, the tracheae are conducting tubes lined with chitin and not thin enough for exchange, and "tracheal system" names the whole network and not the surface itself. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The protein part of a functional enzyme is called:
questions.corrige_markdown: A conjugated enzyme is made of a protein part, the apoenzyme, and a non-protein cofactor (a coenzyme, a prosthetic group or a metal ion activator). The whole functional complex is the holoenzyme: apoenzyme + cofactor. A coenzyme is the organic, non-protein part, and an allosteric enzyme is one that has a second binding site, away from the active site, for a regulator. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which epithelial tissue lines the bladder and ensures that urine does not seep through?
questions.corrige_markdown: The bladder (and the ureters) is lined by transitional epithelium, several layers of cells whose shape can change: the surface cells flatten as the bladder fills and stretches, and the layered, tightly joined cells make a lining that is impermeable to urine. Columnar epithelium lines the gut, cuboidal epithelium the kidney tubules and glands, and pseudostratified ciliated epithelium the trachea. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: This organelle produces the enzyme catalase in most cells:
questions.corrige_markdown: Catalase, which breaks down toxic hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen ($2\,\mathrm{H_2O_2}\rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{H_2O}+\mathrm{O_2}$), is the characteristic enzyme of the microbodies (peroxisomes), which also contain oxidases that make the hydrogen peroxide. The Golgi complex modifies and packages proteins, centrioles organise the spindle, and ribosomes make proteins in general but are not the organelle that is specifically associated with catalase. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Where is cornified epithelium found in a Mammal?
questions.corrige_markdown: Cornified (keratinised) epithelium is stratified squamous epithelium whose outer cells are dead, flattened and filled with the waterproof protein keratin. It forms the surface of the skin (the epidermis), where it protects against abrasion, water loss and microbes. The linings of the buccal cavity, the oesophagus and the vagina are moist stratified squamous epithelium that is not cornified. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In man iodized salts in the food of children prevent:
questions.corrige_markdown: Iodine is a component of the thyroid hormones thyroxine and tri-iodothyronine. A lack of iodine in childhood causes cretinism (stunted growth and mental retardation) and, at any age, goitre, so iodized salt prevents it. Gigantism and acromegaly come from too much growth hormone, in children and adults respectively, and constipation is linked to a lack of dietary fibre. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Enzymes perform their functions because of the following characteristic(s):

- (i) globular proteins..
- (ii) specific in action.
- (iii) lower activation energy.
- (iv) affected by oxygen.
questions.corrige_markdown: (i) is true: enzymes are globular proteins whose folded tertiary structure forms an active site. (ii) is true: the shape of the active site is complementary to one substrate (or a group of similar ones), so each enzyme catalyses a particular reaction. (iii) is true: the enzyme binds the substrate in an enzyme-substrate complex and lowers the activation energy of the reaction. (iv) is false: enzymes are affected by temperature, pH, substrate and enzyme concentration and inhibitors, but oxygen has no general effect on them. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
In humans the respiratory center:

- (i) is stimulated by chemoreceptor in the carotid bodies.
- (ii) is located in the medulla oblongata.
- (iii) controls the rate of breathing.
- (iv) is under voluntary control.
questions.corrige_markdown: (i) is true: chemoreceptors in the carotid (and aortic) bodies detect a rise in carbon dioxide (fall in pH) in the blood and send impulses to the respiratory centre. (ii) is true: the respiratory (breathing) centre is in the medulla oblongata, with a pneumotaxic area in the pons. (iii) is true: it sends impulses along the phrenic and intercostal nerves and so controls the rate and depth of breathing. (iv) is false: the centre works automatically and involuntarily, although the cerebral cortex can modify breathing for a short time. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A pair of genes linked on a single pair of chromosome

- (i) do not assort independently.
- (ii) produce the 9:3:3:1 ratio in the f2.
- (iii) produce the 3:1 ratio in the f2.
- (iv) are transmitted singly in gametes.
questions.corrige_markdown: (i) is true: genes on the same chromosome pair travel together and so do not assort independently. (ii) is false: the 9:3:3:1 ratio of a dihybrid cross is the result of independent assortment of genes on different chromosome pairs. (iii) is true: with complete linkage, an $F_1$ heterozygote in which the dominant alleles are on the same chromosome ($AB/ab$) produces only two kinds of gamete, $AB$ and $ab$, so the $F_2$ is 3 double dominant : 1 double recessive, a 3:1 ratio as in a monohybrid cross. (iv) is false: linked genes are transmitted together in the same gamete (unless crossing over separates them). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following is or are correct of C4 plants?

- (i) Yield is affected by the concentration of oxygen in the atmosphere.
- (ii) Has two kinds of chloroplasts.
- (iii) Requires high concentrations of carbon dioxide.
- (iv) Most have Kranz anatomy.
questions.corrige_markdown: (i) is false: the C$_4$ pathway concentrates carbon dioxide in the bundle sheath cells around RuBisCO, so photorespiration is almost absent and yield is not reduced by atmospheric oxygen (unlike in C$_3$ plants). (ii) is true: mesophyll cells have chloroplasts with grana, while the bundle sheath chloroplasts have few or no grana. (iii) is false: PEP carboxylase has a high affinity for CO$_2$, so C$_4$ plants photosynthesise efficiently at low carbon dioxide concentrations and do not need high concentrations. (iv) is true: most C$_4$ plants (maize, sugar cane) have Kranz anatomy, a ring of bundle sheath cells around the vascular bundle. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
In the eye defect myopia or short sightedness:

- (i) the eye ball is large.
- (ii) image is produced after the retina.
- (iii) a blurred image is produced.
- (iv) correction is by convex lenses.
questions.corrige_markdown: In myopia the eyeball is too long (or the lens too strong), so light from distant objects is focused in front of the retina and the image on the retina is blurred. (i) is true (large, elongated eyeball) and (iii) is true. (ii) is false: an image formed after (behind) the retina is hypermetropia (long sightedness). (iv) is false: myopia is corrected with concave (diverging) lenses, whereas convex lenses correct hypermetropia. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following has a cell wall?

- (i) Plant cell.
- (ii) Animal cell.
- (iii) Bacterial cell.
- (iv) Cheek cell.
questions.corrige_markdown: Plant cells have a cell wall of cellulose and bacterial cells have a wall of peptidoglycan (murein), so (i) and (iii) are correct. Animal cells have only a plasma membrane, and a cheek cell is an animal cell, so (ii) and (iv) are wrong. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following occur(s) in both mitosis and meiosis I?

- (i) Chromosomes form sister chromatids.
- (ii) Nuclear DNA is duplicated during interphase.
- (iii) Chromosomes condense and the nuclear membrane disappears.
- (iv) Chromosomes separate synapse into tetrads.
questions.corrige_markdown: (i) is true: after the DNA is replicated in the S phase each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids, in mitosis and in meiosis I alike. (ii) is true: DNA replication takes place once in the interphase before either division. (iii) is true: in prophase of both divisions the chromosomes condense and the nuclear envelope breaks down. (iv) is false (and badly worded): synapsis, the pairing of homologous chromosomes into bivalents (tetrads), happens only in prophase I of meiosis. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Lateral meristem(s) is (are):

- (i) apical meristem.
- (ii) cork cambium.
- (iii) leaf primodium.
- (iv) vascular cambium.
questions.corrige_markdown: Lateral meristems lie parallel to the sides of stems and roots and cause secondary growth, an increase in girth: the vascular cambium (producing secondary xylem and phloem) and the cork cambium (producing cork), so (ii) and (iv). The apical meristem at the shoot and root tips causes growth in length, and a leaf primordium is a young developing leaf, not a meristem. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The type of growth which shows equal change, in size accompanied by change in shape of an organism is:

*Options as printed:* A) allometric growth.   B) isometric growth.   C) intermittent growth.   D) primary growth.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The stem is self-contradictory. In isometric growth all parts of the organism grow at the same rate, so the size changes but the shape stays the same. In allometric growth different parts grow at different rates, so the size changes and the shape changes too (a human baby, whose head grows less than the limbs; a crab claw). Intermittent growth takes place in stages (arthropods growing between moults) and primary growth is the growth in length of a plant produced by apical meristems. Since the stem asks for growth accompanied by a change in shape, the most probable intended answer is allometric growth, with "equal" being a misprint or a slip for "unequal"; the key cannot be settled from the printed wording.

**Intended answer: A (allometric growth).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of these glands in a mammal is both endocrine and exocrine?
questions.corrige_markdown: The pancreas has an exocrine part (acinar cells secrete the digestive pancreatic juice into the pancreatic duct) and an endocrine part (the islets of Langerhans secrete insulin and glucagon directly into the blood). The pituitary gland is purely endocrine, the sebaceous gland is purely exocrine (sebum into a hair follicle) and the ovary releases hormones into the blood and eggs, which are not a secretion carried by a duct. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Heamophilia is inherited as a sex-linked recessive trait. What is the probability that a woman with a normal father who marries a normal man will have children with this trait? -

*Options as printed:* A) 100%   B) 25%   C) 50%   D) 75%
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $X^H$ be the normal allele and $X^h$ the haemophilia allele. The woman received $X^H$ from her normal father, but the stem does not give the genotype of her mother, so the woman may be $X^HX^H$ (then no child is affected: 0%) or a carrier $X^HX^h$. If she is a carrier and marries a normal man ($X^HY$), the children are $X^HX^H$, $X^HX^h$, $X^HY$ and $X^hY$ in equal numbers: one child in four (25%), a son, is haemophiliac, and no daughter is. Since 0% is not offered, the intended answer is 25%, which assumes the woman is a carrier, but that assumption is not in the printed stem (the question probably meant a father who is haemophiliac).

**Intended answer: B (25%).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following links in a food chain involves the lowest efficient energy transfer?
questions.corrige_markdown: The efficiency of a transfer depends on how much of the energy in the food is assimilated and built into new tissue. Dead mangrove leaves consist largely of cellulose, lignin and tannins, which small crustaceans digest poorly, so most of the energy is lost in the faeces and only a small fraction is passed on. Animal prey (tilapia, dolphins) is rich in easily digested protein and fat and is assimilated with a much higher efficiency, so links A, B and C are more efficient. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Small crustaceans feed on dead mangrove leaves.

questions.enonce_markdown: Resting potential is maintained by:
questions.corrige_markdown: The resting potential of a neurone (about $-70$ mV inside) is maintained by the sodium-potassium pump, which uses ATP to move 3 Na$^+$ out and 2 K$^+$ in (active transport), and by the facilitated diffusion of K$^+$ out through open potassium leak channels, because the membrane is much more permeable to K$^+$ than to Na$^+$. Osmosis is the movement of water and plays no part, and voltage-gated channels are closed at rest (they open during the action potential). **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: active transport and voltage gated ion channels.

questions.enonce_markdown: A woman with blood group O can never have a child with:
questions.corrige_markdown: A woman of group O has the genotype $ii$, so every egg carries the allele $i$. Her child receives $I^A$, $I^B$ or $i$ from the father and $i$ from her, so it can be $I^Ai$ (group A), $I^Bi$ (group B) or $ii$ (group O). Group AB needs one $I^A$ and one $I^B$, and she can supply neither. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In the biotechnical process, the step requiring the search and possible genetic engineering of a suitable organism is called:
questions.corrige_markdown: In an industrial biotechnological process the first step is screening: looking for (and isolating) micro-organisms that make the wanted product, and if necessary improving them by mutation or genetic engineering. The chosen strain is then grown in larger volumes (scaling up), the process runs in the fermenter, and the product is finally recovered and purified (downstream processing). Cloning means making identical copies of cells, organisms or genes. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In ferns, the gametophyte generation consist of:
questions.corrige_markdown: In a fern the conspicuous, dominant plant with fronds, rhizome and roots is the sporophyte (the fronds bear spore-producing sori; "son" in option A is a misprint for sori). The spores germinate into the gametophyte, a small, flat, heart-shaped, green prothallus anchored by rhizoids, which bears the antheridia and archegonia. So the gametophyte consists of the prothallus and its rhizoids. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
In human females, the first polar body:

*Options as printed:* A) is not produced until fertilization occurs.   B) divides to give the second polar body.   C) is formed at ovulation.   D) is formed only if fertilization occurs.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The first polar body is the small cell produced at the end of meiosis I, when the primary oocyte becomes a secondary oocyte; this is triggered by the LH surge just before ovulation, so the first polar body is present at ovulation, together with the secondary oocyte, which is arrested at metaphase II. The first polar body may itself divide to give two polar bodies, and the second polar body of the oocyte is formed only after fertilization, when meiosis II is completed. Options A and D therefore describe the second polar body and are false for the first. Options B and C are both defensible, as the first polar body is formed at about the time of ovulation and may divide. The printed options are also overprinted and hard to read, so no letter is marked as correct.



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: An anti microbial substance produced by some bacteria is called:
questions.corrige_markdown: An antibiotic is a chemical substance produced by a micro-organism (some bacteria such as Streptomyces, and fungi such as Penicillium) that kills or inhibits the growth of other micro-organisms. Toxins are poisons made by pathogens, pathogens are disease-causing organisms, and carcinogens are agents that cause cancer. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Natural selection is also known as:
questions.corrige_markdown: Natural selection, the mechanism proposed by Darwin and Wallace, is the process by which individuals better adapted to their environment survive and reproduce more, so their favourable alleles increase in the next generation. It is popularly summed up as "survival of the fittest". Adaptive radiation, convergent evolution and speciation are results of evolution and not other names for the mechanism. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which gland in mammals produces cortisol?
questions.corrige_markdown: Cortisol is a glucocorticoid hormone secreted by the cortex of the adrenal gland (on top of the kidney) under the control of ACTH from the pituitary. It is released in stress, raises blood glucose by promoting gluconeogenesis, and suppresses inflammation. The parathyroid gland makes parathormone, the thyroid thyroxine and calcitonin, and the pituitary releases ACTH and other tropic hormones. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What are autosomes?
questions.corrige_markdown: Autosomes are all the chromosomes of a cell except the sex chromosomes (X and Y); humans have 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes. They are the ordinary "somatic" chromosomes, as opposed to the sex chromosomes. Option B is wrong because mitochondrial DNA is not organised into autosomes, option C describes chromosome mutations, and option D, although all chromosomes (the sex chromosomes too) are found in the nucleus, does not distinguish autosomes from sex chromosomes. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Chromosomes found only in the mitochondria.
Chromosome abnormalities that result in genetic defects.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**First statement:** Ventilation in mammals is initiated by the concentration of carbon dioxide in bipod [sic: blood].

**Second statement:** Ventilation in mammals end up with gaseous exchange at the alveoli.
questions.corrige_markdown: The first statement is true (reading "bipod" as blood): a rise in the carbon dioxide concentration of the blood, which lowers its pH, is detected by chemoreceptors in the medulla and in the carotid and aortic bodies; they stimulate the breathing centre, which sends impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles. The second statement is also true: ventilation brings fresh air to the alveoli, where gaseous exchange takes place. However, the second gives the result of ventilation and not the reason why carbon dioxide concentration starts it, so it does not explain the first. **Answer: B.**

**First statement:** Enzymes are said to be specific in their biochemical reactions.

**Second statement:** Enzymes are globular proteins with specific conformational 3D structures.
questions.corrige_markdown: Both statements are true. questions.enonce_markdown:
**First statement:** Photosystem II harvest more light energy than photosystem I during photosynthesis.

**Second statement:** Photosystem II is found in the grana of chloroplast.

*Options as printed:* A) Both statements are true and the second explains the first   B) Both statements are true but the second does not explain the first   C) The first statement is true and the second is false   D) The first statement is false and the second is true
questions.corrige_markdown:
The second statement is true: photosystem II (P680) is located mostly in the thylakoids of the grana, while photosystem I is found mainly in the stroma lamellae. The first statement is not a standard textbook statement. It can be defended, since photosystem II has the larger light-harvesting antenna (the LHCII complexes, rich in chlorophyll b) and absorbs light of shorter wavelength (680 nm) and therefore higher energy per photon than photosystem I (700 nm). It can also be rejected, as both photosystems absorb light and the amount of energy they harvest is not compared in the usual syllabus. Taken as true, the position in the grana does not explain the amount of light harvested, which gives B; taken as false, the answer is D. The key cannot be settled from the printed wording.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**First statement:** Carbon monoxide is a powerful respiratory poison.

**Second statement:** Carbon monoxide is odourless.
questions.corrige_markdown: Both statements are true. Carbon monoxide combines irreversibly with haemoglobin, with an affinity about 250 times that of oxygen, to form stable carboxyhaemoglobin, so the blood can no longer carry enough oxygen, and it also inhibits cytochrome oxidase in the respiratory chain. It is a colourless, odourless gas, which makes it dangerous because it is not detected, but this does not explain why it is a poison. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**First statement:** The stratified epithelium of the skin is cornified.

**Second statement:** The stratified epithelium is lying on a basement membrane.
questions.corrige_markdown: Both statements are true. The epidermis is a stratified squamous epithelium whose outer cells are filled with keratin and dead (cornified), and, like every epithelium, it rests on a basement membrane that anchors it to the connective tissue. The basement membrane has nothing to do with the keratinisation of the surface cells, so the second does not explain the first. **Answer: B.**

**First statement:** In mosses the sporophyte generation is dominant.

**Second statement:** The sporophyte generation of moss consist of capsule, seta and foot.
questions.corrige_markdown: The first statement is false: in mosses (bryophytes) the dominant, conspicuous generation is the leafy gametophyte, and the sporophyte is short-lived and depends on it.
